profile.summary: Naum is a short but intense prophecy directed to the scene of imperial threat surrounding Judah. The book answers the question whether God can act when an oppressive people seem invincible: yes, He judges violence, governs history and helps the afflicted. The message combines a proclamation of judgment against Nineveh and comfort for Judah, showing that the power of Assyria, though enormous in human eyes, would not escape the divine scrutiny. At the same time, the book preserves hope: God's righteousness is not only the destruction of evil, but also the restoration of peace and worship for his people.
profile.setting: The backdrop is the end of the 7th century BC, when the kingdom of Judah lived under the threat of the Assyrian empire, whose capital was Nineveh. The introduction situates the prophecy after the fall of Thebes and before the fall of Nineveh, between 663 and 612 BC, but the exact date within that interval is uncertain. The author is identified as Naum, the echtyham, but it is not known for certain whether Elcos was a clan or locality; the most likely hypothesis is that it was a city in the southwest of Judah. The political context includes Assyrian pressure on Judah and the reign of Manasseh, with his past of infidelity still leaving marks on the people. Literarily, the book alternates oracles of judgment, vivid descriptions of the ruin of Nineveh and brief satirical ironies against the imperial city.

structure.label: Opening: the character of God and the beginning of the announcement
structure.description: The chapter begins with the presentation of the power, justice and goodness of God, establishing the tone of prophecy and the principle that the Lord knows and governs history.

structure.label: Annoyed Fall of Nineveh and reversal of the threat
structure.description: The second chapter focuses on the siege and ruin of the Assyrian capital, with the contrast between the defeat of the oppressor and the tranquility restored to Judah.

structure.label: Final description of the judgment and theironic outcome
structure.description: The third chapter resumes and deepens Nineveh's condemnation, highlighting his vulnerability, his shame and the impossibility of escape or help.

themes: Sovereignty of God over the nations and about history
Divine judgment against violence and oppression
Comfort and hope for the people of God
God's patience and the assurance that righteousness will prevail
readingKeys: Notice how the book alternates threat and comfort: the same God who breaks down the oppressor protects the oppressed.
Pay attention to the poetic and satirical images; they are not ornamented, but a central part of the prophet's argumentation.
Read the book in the light of the contrast between Nineveh's apparent strength and the Lord's silent but aside authority.
profile.cautions: Authorship is traditionally attributed to Naum, but besides this identification the book does not offer many biographical data; the location of Elcos is also uncertain. The date of prophecy remains debated within the interval between the fall of Thebes and Nineveh. Reading should avoid reducing the book the mere national revenge: the introduction presents it from everything as an affirmation of the righteous government of God, which judges violence and comforts the afflicted.

dossier.narratedEra: Later Neo-Assyrian period, with the Assyrian threat to Judah and the Near East, in the interval between the fall of Thebes (663 BC) and the fall of Nineveh (612 BC). The setting of the book is the political and military crisis surrounding the Assyrian empire, especially under Ashurbanipal, with vulnerable Judah and already exiled Israel.
dossier.compositionEra: The composition is located in the notes between 663 and 612 BC. The most likely proposal in the sources is that Naum prophesied at some point in this interval; there is debate about whether it was at the end of the reign of Manasseh (c. 648-665 BC, possibly after his release from Assyrian captivity) or at the beginning/middle of the reign of Josiah (640-609 BC). Matthew Henry also features another academic conjecture: perhaps 1:1-2:2 and the other chapters have been uttered at different times, with chapters 2-3 maybe a few years later.

politics.title: Ascension and apogee of Assyrian power under Ashurbanipal
politics.detail: The notes place Nineveh as the capital of the Assyrian Empire after 705 BC, and describe Ashurbanipal (668-626 BC) as the one that led Assyrian power to its peak, with military force and cultural influence throughout the Ancient Near East.
politics.readingImpact: This shows that prophecy does not speak of a peripheral enemy, but from the center of imperial power. The threat to Judah was real, and the claim that God will judge Nineveh gains concrete political weight.

politics.title: Judah at risk of imperial absorption
politics.detail: At Naum's time, Judah was in danger of being swallowed up by the Assyrian empire. The introduction emphasizes that this scenario made the message of judgment against Nineveh at the same time warning to the oppressors and comfort to the oppressed.
politics.readingImpact: Reading ceases to be only distant oracle and becomes a word of resistance to a small kingdom surrounded by superpower.

politics.title: Israel had fallen to Assyria
politics.detail: The notes recall that the northern kingdom fell into the hands of the Assyrians in 722 BC, and that the "ten tribes" had already been taken captive. Matthew Henry associates this with the comfort directed to those tribes and God's people in general.
politics.readingImpact: The announcement of Nineveh's fall is not only vengeance, but a sign that God responds to the devastation already suffered by Israel.

politics.title: Manasseh, vassalage and political wound in Judah
politics.detail: Tyndale's introduction states that Ashurbanipal captured King Manasseh and took him to Babylon; after he was released, Manasseh attempted to reverse his ancient wickedness, but his influence remained on the earth. The notes of 1:12 also say that Judah was previously punished in the 701 BC campaign, although it was not defeated by Assyria.
politics.readingImpact: This background intensifies the tone of the book: Naum speaks to a nation wounded by imperial pressure and inner sin, not to a politically stable people.

politics.title: The fall of Nineveh as a geopolitical turn
politics.detail: The notes claim that after Ashurbanipal's death in 626 BC, Assyria cities began to fall one by one and Nineveh fell in 612 BC. The fall was attributed to the joint advance of Chaldeans, fears and ummanda.
politics.readingImpact: The reader is led to see prophecy as a verifiable historical proclamation on the book's own horizon, reinforcing divine sovereignty over empires.

politics.title: Thebes as Imperial counterpoint
politics.detail: The notes highlight Thebes as the former Egyptian capital still prosperous, but conquered by Ashurbanipal in 663 BC. The mention is of precedent for the ruin of Nineveh.
politics.readingImpact: The text uses the historical logic of "I've already happened to Thebes" to dismantle Nineveh's false invulnerability.

customs.title: Life under taxation, trade and imperial estate
customs.detail: The notes say that riches of other peoples flowed to Nineveh through trade, tribute and spoil. The empire accumulated wealth by exploitation and war.
customs.readingImpact: The economic image explains why Nineveh's condemnation includes not only military violence, but also structural injustice and plunder.

customs.title: Assyrian war culture and daily brutality of war
customs.detail: The notes describe assyrian practices of cruelty: amputation of limbs, cluttering, display of heads, blinding and skinning. In 3:2-3, the chariots and their drivers are remembered as feared everywhere.
customs.readingImpact: The language of the book gains moral and pastoral weight: divine judgment is not abstract, but a response to a culture of terror routinely practiced.

customs.title: Siege, urban defenses and water engineering
customs.detail: At 2:1, the notes mention ramps, roads, fortifications and defense forces. In 2:6, Nineveh is described with a reservoir formed by a double dam on the Khosr River, with floodgates; the rain would have increased the river system and the invaders released the water against the walls.
customs.readingImpact: The siege appears as a historically concrete event, not as a vague metaphor. The city seems strong, but its own infrastructure becomes an instrument of ruin.

customs.title: Public fear and signs of humiliation
customs.detail: The notes note that "beating in the chest" was a common sign of mourning and that the escape of the inhabitants occurs in panic in the face of the fall of the city.
customs.readingImpact: The reader realizes that prophecy portrays not only military defeat, but also the social and emotional collapse of a city in mourning.

customs.title: Imperial economy and abandonment in times of crisis
customs.detail: Tyndale claims that Assyrian merchants spread across the Near East as locusts, accumulating wealth in Nineveh; but in the time of calamity they would leave, leaving the people in need. The image of the provisions and the loot is central in 3:15-17.
customs.readingImpact: The prophecy denounces the prosperity built on exploitation and shows its fragility when the judgment arrives.

customs.title: Urban life in Nineveh marked by pride and self-confidence
customs.detail: The notes describe the sarcastic appeal for the city to prepare, strengthen and strengthen its defenses, which shows public confidence in human and military resources.
customs.readingImpact: The scene transforms reading into criticism of political self-security: the city invests everything in defense, but this does not alter the divine decree.

language.title: Name of Naum as "comfort/ennial"
language.detail: Tyndale says that the name Naum means "comfort" or "encouragement"; Matthew Henry also notes that his name means comforting.
language.readingImpact: The reader understands the book as a comfort to the people of God, even when the immediate content is of terror to the Assyrians.

language.title: Poetic anthem in two stanzas over the sovereign power of God
language.detail: The notes divide 1:2-11 into two poetic hymns: 1:2-6 and 1:7-11. The first stanza echoes texts of the exodus; the second highlights sovereignty, justice and refuge for those who trust in the Lord.
language.readingImpact: The poetic structure guides reading: before speaking of Nineveh, the book fixes the identity of God as a judge and refuge.

language.title: Images of storm, sea, mountains and tremendous land
language.detail: The notes explain that the book uses image of divine fury as a whirlwind, storm, clouds, seas, rivers, mountains and land that shakes. There is also reference to the contrast with Canaanite mythologies over the domination of the waters.
language.readingImpact: These images broaden the scale of judgment: it is not only a local event, but a cosmic performance of the God who governs creation.

language.title: Trot satirical and sarcasm against Nineveh
language.detail: In 2:11-13 and 3:14-19, notes identify the use of mockery and sarcasm songs. The tone is deliberately ironic: the city is ordered to prepare, but its preparation is useless.
language.readingImpact: The reader is led to hear the ruin of Nineveh as public humiliation, not just as a war defeat.

language.title: Alliteration and sound effect at 2:10
language.detail: The notes point to the alliterated Hebrew sequence to "disposed, empty and destroyed," highlighting the devastation sound effect.
language.readingImpact: The appeal reinforces the intensity of judgment and suggests speed and totality of ruin.

language.title: Metaphors of lion, locusts, wolves, and sheep
language.detail: Nineveh is compared to the den of lions; later merchants and armies are portrayed as locusts; without the leaders, the people are scattered like sheep, while the chiefs of lions in death.
language.readingImpact: The images make judgment vivid and moral: the ferocious predator reveals himself mortally vulnerable, and the unleavened population becomes helpless.

timeline.title: 663 BC: fall of Thebes
timeline.detail: The notes place the fall of Thebes under Ashurbanipal in 663 BC and state that Naum mentions it as a precedent of the judgment against Nineveh.
timeline.readingImpact: This date works as a textual landmark to date the prophecy and also as proof that neither the great capitals escape judgment.

timeline.title: Between 663 and 612 BC: General Window of Prophecy
timeline.detail: The introduction states that Naum spoke at some point between the fall of Thebes and the fall of Nineveh.
timeline.readingImpact: The book should be read within this historical range, without projecting it to later or earlier periods without the basis of the notes.

timeline.title: Possible date at the end of Manasseh's reign
timeline.detail: Tyndale proposes that Naum may have prophesied around 648-665 BC, after the return of Manasseh from Assyrian captivity and during his attempts to reform.
timeline.readingImpact: If this hypothesis is followed, the prophecy arises in the context of a Judah shaken by oppression and attempted moral restoration.

timeline.title: Another possibility: beginning or amidst the reign of Josiah
timeline.detail: The notes also say that the prophecy may have been given later, in the beginning or a half of the reign of Josiah (640-609 BC).
timeline.readingImpact: This alternative puts the book in a phase of political and religious transition in Judah, but still under Assyrian shadow.

timeline.title: 626 BC: Ashurbanipal death and Assyrian weakening
timeline.detail: The introduction says that after Ashurbanipal's death in 626 BC, the Assyrian cities began to fall one after another.
timeline.readingImpact: This milestone gives meaning to the urgency of prophecy: the empire was already in erosion when the word was announced.

timeline.title: 612 BC: Nineveh fall
timeline.detail: Both the introduction and the notes of 1:14 claim that Nineveh fell in 612 BC, according to the prophetic announcement.
timeline.readingImpact: The reading receives historical confirmation within the horizon presented by the notes itself; the announced judgment was not rhetorical, but it came to occur.

investigation: The sources provided are introductions and evangelical Protestant study notes; they offer theological and historical interpretation, not independent historical proof.
There is an important distinction between the setting of the book (Assyrian period with threat to Judah) and the exact date of composition, which remains debated in the notes.

Matthew Henry suggests a development in stages of the prophetic material and connects the date most likely to Hezekiah's time, while Tyndale prefers a wider window between 663 and 612 BC with options at the end of Manasses or Josiah start/hence.

The notes focus almost entirely on Nineveh, Assyria, Thebes and Judah; they do not offer detailed data on family, domestic economy, meals or social classes in a broad way, only images and punctual allusions.
Literary images are explored in a devotional and contextual way, but etymologies and technical translations were only included when explicitly mentioned in the notes.

Some historical reconstructions, such as the use of waters of the Khosr river against the walls of Nineveh, appear as a note explanation; here they were treated as affirmation of the secondary source, not as external verification.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends entirely on the attached notes and therefore is selective: it only includes information that these sources directly explain or interpret directly. No exact dates have been added other than those mentioned in the notes, nor were developed archaeological contexts, alternative chronologies or biographical details of Naum that do not appear in the sources. The coverage of customs is limited because the notes deal more of war, siege, grief, trade and imperial propaganda than of broad everyday life. There is also controversy of dating: the sources do not fully agree on the moment of composition, and this was preserved as a debate, without its own resolution. Finally, confessional readings of the notes were maintained in a contextual perspective, but without broadening doctrinal conclusions beyond what the material provided supports.
